topic: More reports do not always mean more wildlife
grammarFocus: 学术论证的限定、因果、对比与证据范围
title: More reports do not always mean more wildlife
instructions: 原创学术微训练；场景、机构与数值均为虚构模拟，不是事实报道或官方试题。先独立阅读答题，再用原句核对限定、比较与因果。短篇专项不能替代完整陌生测评。
passage:
A. A fictional citizen-science project invited residents to record birds seen from their windows. Reports increased sharply after a local radio campaign. The organiser wanted to announce that bird numbers had grown. A volunteer statistician explained that the number of reports depended both on birds and on the effort people made to observe them.

B. During the first month, forty households contributed. During the campaign month, one hundred and ten did. Some new volunteers also spent longer watching because the programme encouraged a weekend observation session. More sightings could therefore occur even if the local bird population remained unchanged. A report count was valuable evidence of participation, but not automatically of population growth.

C. The project revised its form to ask for observation duration and the type of setting, such as a balcony or garden. It also asked contributors to submit a record when they watched but saw no birds. Without those zero observations, the dataset would contain sightings without showing how often an opportunity produced none. A missing record could not safely be treated as the same thing as a recorded zero.

D. Identification created another problem. An unfamiliar bird might be reported under a common species name. Volunteers could attach photographs, and doubtful records were flagged for later checking. A flagged record was neither confirmed nor necessarily false. The public map used separate symbols for confirmed and unverified sightings so that uncertainty remained visible.

E. The organiser's revised announcement celebrated wider participation and explained that trends in bird numbers required more comparable observations. The project still welcomed casual reports because they could highlight places worth investigating. It simply distinguished exploratory information from evidence suitable for estimating change. For the following season, volunteers were invited to repeat a fixed ten-minute session each week. Consistency would make the records more informative without requiring every participant to become a professional observer.
